# Draft:Cultural Heritage Partners, PLLC

Overview
Cultural Heritage Partners, PLLC (CHP) is an American law firm with a global practice in cultural heritage law. The firm helps clients protect and preserve archaeology, architecture, landscapes, art, burial grounds, sacred spaces, traditional knowledge and practices, sovereignty, and related civil and human rights. CHP's clients include Indigenous nations, African American communities, historic cities and towns, cultural institutions, and preservation advocacy organizations. The firm has offices in Richmond, Virginia, and Washington, DC. In addition to lawyers, it has employed scientists; scholars; and practitioners in archaeology, art, history, and Indigenous relations.
History
Marion F. Werkheiser, Greg Werkheiser, and Donald Craib founded Cultural Heritage Partners in 2010.
Notable Cases and Matters
CHP has been involved in legal matters concerning national and international disputes over cultural property and heritage governance.
'''Challenging President Donald Trump’s Plans to Alter Washington, DC's Historic Landscape (2025-present)'''
In February 2026, President Trump announced plans to gut the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and use only the existing frame to rebuild. Representing a coalition of national preservation and architectural organizations, CHP filed a federal lawsuit seeking an injunction against demolition or substantial alteration of the Kennedy Center unless and until the Administration complied with the expert and public consultation requirements of the National Historic Preservation Act and the National Environmental Policy  Act.
Similarly, in 2025, CHP and its founders filed a federal lawsuit seeking to enjoin the Trump Administration from altering the historic exterior of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB), a National Historic Landmark adjacent to the White House without first complying with the same federal consultation processes. The President stated his preference for painting the exterior gray granite bright white, which experts have said would permanently harm the structural integrity of the building, in addition to changing its historic appearance. The Administration agreed to refrain from altering the EEOB while the case is pending.
CHP's EEOB lawsuit was the first in a series to challenge the President's efforts to reshape Washington’s historic landscape, including suits challenging the construction of a ballroom following the demolition of the White House East Wing, takeover of the East Potomac Park golf course, renaming the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, and plans to erect a large arch at Arlington National Cemetery’s Memorial Circle.
Compelling the Army to Repatriate Indian Boarding School Burials (2024-present)
CHP and the Native American Rights Fund represented the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska in litigation against the U.S. Army concerning the repatriation of children buried at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School cemetery. The complaint alleged noncompliance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act and sought enforcement of statutory obligations requiring the return of remains to descendant communities.
Resolving Adverse Impacts of Offshore Wind Farms (2016-present)
As offshore wind development expanded in the United States, CHP represented historic coastal communities—including Nantucket, Cape May County. Block Island, and Newport—in the first proceedings challenging permitting practices by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management. The matters questioned whether the federal government and developers had properly balanced the risks posed by industrialized seascapes to communities with heritage tourism-based economies. CHP's Greg Werkheiser said, "We can't have it both ways. We [can't] bend the rules for one industry and not expect that to be harmful when other industries say, 'well, if it's good enough for offshore wind, why isn't it good enough for coal or fracking?' " CHP has negotiated community benefit agreements to secure greater protection for historic communities than provided for in the permitting process.
The firm also represented Nantucket following the July 2024 failure of a turbine blade in the Vineyard Wind project, which dispersed fiberglass debris onto the island’s beaches during peak tourism season. In 2025, the firm secured a $10.5 million settlement from turbine manufacturer GE Vernova to compensate the town and affected businesses.
Strengthening Newly Federally Recognized Tribal Nations in Virginia (2018-2024)
CHP represented the six American Indian tribes recognized by Congress through the Thomasina E. Jordan Indian Tribes of Virginia Federal Recognition Act of 2017. Upon federal acknowledgement as sovereign nations, CHP helped the tribes reformat their governments, invest in physical infrastructure and community outreach, navigate the COVID-19 pandemic, protect cultural resources, and seek improved understanding of their history and status by state government and state and federal judges.
CHP represented the tribes in negotiations with the Office of Governor Ralph Northam, which led to Governor Northam’s Executive Order 82 requiring consultation with tribes on certain state permits, later codified.
'Recovering the Stolen Wounded Indian Sculpture (2023)'
CHP represented the Massachusetts Charitable Mechanic Association in the recovery of Wounded Indian (1850), a life-sized marble sculpture by Peter Stephenson. The Association, founded in the 18th century by Paul Revere and other artisans, received the sculpture as a donation in 1893. It was believed to have been destroyed during a 1958 building relocation but later resurfaced intact in the collection of Norfolk, Virginia’s Chrysler Museum of Art after being donated by a private collector.
Following extended legal efforts, the museum agreed in 2023 to return the sculpture. The case underscored the importance of provenance research and institutional due diligence in museum collections management.
Securing Power for Descendants at James Madison’s Montpelier (2021-2022)
CHP represented the Montpelier Descendants Committee in efforts to obtain shared governance of James Madison's Montpelier, the historic home of President James Madison and burial site of more than 300 people he enslaved. In 2022, the Montpelier Foundation rescinded a power-sharing agreement and dismissed staff members who supported descendant participation, prompting national attention to governance and interpretive authority at historic institutions.
Following negotiations and public advocacy, Montpelier restructured its board, elected descendant representatives to a majority, reinstated terminated staff, and appointed a new president and board chairman. The restructuring was widely described as the first formal shared-governance model between a major U.S. historic site and descendants of enslaved persons.
Securing Passage of the African-American Burial Grounds Preservation Act (2022)
CHP led national advocacy efforts on behalf of more than 150 organizations for federal legislation establishing a national framework to identify, preserve, and interpret historic African American burial grounds. In 2022, Congress enacted the African- American Burial Grounds Preservation Act, creating a voluntary national network and grant program administered by the National Park Service to support research, technical assistance, and public education regarding African American cemeteries and burial sites.
The statute addressed longstanding gaps in documentation and protection of historically marginalized burial grounds and formalized a federal role in coordinating preservation efforts.
Preserving New Market Heights Battlefield (2022)
New Market Heights was the site of a significant Civil War battle, resulting in 14 of the 16 Medal of Honor awards given to Black recipients during the war. When the site was slated to be developed into a housing development, CHP represented advocates and saved the battleground.
Saving the Ancient Monacan Capital of Rassawek (2018-2022)
CHP represented the Monacan Indian Nation in efforts to preserve Rassawek, the tribe’s historic capital depicted on John Smith’s 1612 map of Virginia. The site, which contains Native burials, was threatened by plans to construct a regional water pumping station. In 2020, the National Trust for Historic Preservation named Rassawek one of America’s Most Endangered Historic Places. After several years of advocacy, local governments selected an alternative site for development, and Rassawek was preserved.
The matter represented the first major test of the collective influence of Virginia’s recently federally recognized Tribal Nations in asserting authority to protect ancestral sites within federal regulatory processes.
Removing Confederate Monuments from Public Property (2020-2022)
CHP developed the legal strategy used by Levar Stoney, mayor of Richmond, Virginia, to remove more than a dozen Confederate monuments from city property, including along Monument Avenue, during the 2020 protests following the murder of George Floyd. Richmond’s monuments were among the most prominent "Lost Cause" monuments in the United States.
The firm subsequently represented 50 families whose homes had views of the state-owned monument to Robert E. Lee in litigation that contributed to its removal. The firm later facilitated transfer of ownership of the monuments to the Black History Museum and Cultural Center of Virginia.
Separately, the firm defended the City of Charleston, South Carolina, as it removed monuments and renamed public spaces, securing dismissal of the lawsuits seeking to reverse those changes.
Restoring State Recognition of Tribes Withdrawn by New Jersey (2012-2019)
CHP represented tribal governments in litigation challenging the withdrawal of state recognition during the administration of Governor Chris Christie. The suits alleged violations of federal and state due-process and equal-protection guarantees. After several years of litigation, New Jersey reaffirmed tribal recognition and entered into a monetary settlement. The case established a precedent that states cannot arbitrarily rescind tribal recognition after decades of prior acknowledgment.
Managing Preservation50 (2015-2016)
In 2016, the National Historic Preservation Act turned 50, and an unprecedented alliance of preservation organizations worked together to commemorate the achievements of the first 50 years of historic preservation successes and to plan for the future. CHP led the planning and advocacy efforts for nationwide celebrations, discourse, and legislation.
Preventing Cultural Racketeering (2015-present)
CHP has advised foreign governments, notably the government of Egypt, and cultural institutions on matters involving repatriation, archaeological stewardship, site management, and dispute resolution involving cultural property. Firm personnel have been involved in cases to reclaim Nazi-looted art.
In 2015, firm co-founder Marion Werkheiser participated in the ministerial-level conference with 10 countries and UNESCO, from which was issued the Cairo Declaration aimed to stop terrorist financing through cultural racketeering.
Other Matters
Opposing the Trump Administration’s Targeting of Law Firms (2025)
In 2025, CHP joined an amicus brief supporting Perkins Coie in its challenge to Executive Order 14230, which was part of a pattern of the targeting of law firms and lawyers under the second Trump Administration. A federal court struck down the order as violating the First Amendment. The Trump Administration has appealed.
